correctness.rationale: A binary de Bruijn cycle of order5 is uniquely rooted at its 00000 window. Hamiltonian circuits in the five-bit shift-and-append graph rooted at zero biject the rotation classes; a separate direct DFS independently enumerated all 2048 unique cycles and explicitly checked 32 distinct cyclic length-five windows for each. For every 32-symbol linear rotation, the shortest absent binary-subsequence DP and greedily terminated full-alphabet arches computed identical universality indices. All 2048 times32 rotations were evaluated, giving exactly 512 cycles circular index10 and 1536 index11; canonical split (iota,zeta): (9,10)256,(10,10)256,(10,11)1152,(11,11)384. The independent complement/reversal orbit tally is 16 and120 (sizes2,4) at zeta10 and 16 and376 at zeta11. The source's distinct Euler-edge enumerator provides a second traversal check. This is a genuinely exhaustive finite proof for exactly order5; it is not an all-order inference or sampling claim.

originality.rationale: De Bruijn's classical 2048 count and the Hamiltonian/Eulerian bijections are old. Hébrard's arch factorization and Barker et al. Definition4/Lemma20 establish the circular universality invariant and general inequalities, while Fleischmann et al. treat circular universality of general words; none of the inspected full texts presents the conditional spectrum for all order5 de Bruijn cycles. A Resultary record gives a closed-form finite-length universality distribution for *unrestricted* binary words (different conditioning), not for 2048 de Bruijn cycles. No exact 512/1536 order-five table was recovered; historical priority remains limited by potential unindexed specialized tables and older Hébrard full text.

value.rationale: De Bruijn cycles are optimal contiguous factor covers, but scattered-subsequence universality after deletions is an independent natural coverage metric used for word universality and robust test patterns. A complete tally at the first order exhibiting a nonuniform circular index spectrum—one quarter at10, three quarters at11—can guide selection of deletion-resilient de Bruijn test cycles and benchmark algorithms. The precise full-order-five spectrum is a natural finite classification and is not merely a random slice, copied sequence table, or unmotivated arithmetic experiment. No all-order general theorem or downstream application is claimed.
